_comment: Seed content for the Tree of the Day pack. Lives OUTSIDE src/ on purpose: it holds answers, and nothing under src/ should be able to import it via the @/ alias and drag it into a client bundle. Consumed only by scripts/seed-pack.mjs. Hints are ordered easy -> hard and deliberately never contain the answer or any closeTerm.

hints: A slender, short-lived tree of northern woods and heathland, usually among the first to colonise bare ground.
The trunk is strikingly pale, almost white, and peels in fine papery horizontal strips.
Small triangular leaves flutter on thin stalks, and the outer twigs droop enough to give the crown a weeping outline.
Diamond-shaped black fissures crack the pale bark towards the base of older trunks.
Its Latin species name, pendula, refers to those drooping twigs. It is the national tree of Finland.
puzzles.fact: A pioneer species: its light, wind-blown seed lets it colonise cleared ground within a season, improving the soil for the slower, longer-lived trees that follow it.

hints: A broad, heavy-limbed tree that grows wider than it is tall in open ground, and can live a thousand years.
Its timber built medieval warships and cathedral roofs across northern Europe.
The leaves are deeply lobed with almost no stalk, and two small ear-like lobes clasp the twig.
The fruit is a smooth nut sitting in a scaly cup, carried on a long stalk.
Its species name robur means strength, and single ancient specimens are named landmarks in England.
puzzles.fact: It supports more species of insect, lichen and fungus than any other tree in Britain — over 2,000 have been recorded on it, more than 300 of which are found on nothing else.

hints: Almost always planted beside water, where the reflection is half the point.
Long narrow leaves hang from branches that fall in curtains right to the ground.
Snapped twigs root readily in wet mud, so it spreads easily from broken fragments.
Bark from this genus was the traditional source of the compound that became aspirin.
Its Latin name wrongly credits Babylon; it actually came west from northern China along the silk routes.
puzzles.fact: The species name babylonica is a mistake. Linnaeus linked it to the biblical willows of Babylon, but the tree originates in northern China and reached Europe via the silk routes.

hints: A large hardwood of eastern North America, best known for what it does in autumn.
Its five-lobed leaf is a national emblem.
The sap is tapped in late winter, when nights still freeze and days thaw.
Paired winged seeds spin to the ground like helicopter blades.
Roughly forty litres of its sap boil down to a single litre of syrup.
puzzles.fact: It takes around 40 litres of sap to make one litre of syrup, which is why a mature stand is tapped for decades rather than felled. Trees are usually 40 years old before the first tap.

hints: A tree with no close living relatives at all — the sole survivor of an entire plant division.
Fan-shaped leaves with parallel veins and a notch in the middle turn uniform butter-yellow, then drop almost all at once.
Fossils nearly identical to it are found in rocks 200 million years old.
The fleshy seed coat of the female tree smells strongly of rancid butter, so cities plant only males.
Several specimens within two kilometres of the Hiroshima blast survived it and are still alive.
puzzles.fact: A living fossil with no close living relatives. Six trees within two kilometres of the Hiroshima hypocentre survived the 1945 blast, resprouted the following spring, and are still growing.

hints: The tallest living thing on Earth.
It grows in a narrow fog belt along one stretch of Pacific coastline.
Thick fibrous bark, sometimes a foot deep, resists fire and is a deep rusty colour.
It absorbs fog directly through its foliage, which supplies much of its summer water.
The tallest known individual, named Hyperion, stands over 115 metres.
puzzles.fact: The tallest known individual, Hyperion, exceeds 115 metres. Its exact location is kept secret, because foot traffic around the base compacts the shallow roots the tree depends on.

hints: A hardy conifer with the widest natural range in its genus, from Spain to Siberia.
The needles come in twisted pairs and are distinctly blue-green.
The upper trunk and branches glow orange in low sun, against grey bark lower down.
Old open-grown trees drop their lower limbs and take on a flat, umbrella-like crown.
It is the last remnant of the Caledonian forest and the national tree of Scotland.
puzzles.fact: The only pine native to northern Europe. The Caledonian forest fragments it forms in the Highlands are the surviving remains of woodland that once covered much of Scotland.

hints: A big domed park and avenue tree, planted mainly for its spring flower spikes.
White flower candles stand upright all over the crown in May.
The leaves are palmate — five to seven leaflets radiating from a single point like fingers.
Glossy brown nuts fall inside spiky green cases and are used in a children's playground game.
Its seeds are mildly toxic, and it is not related to the edible nut it is named after.
puzzles.fact: Despite the name it is unrelated to the edible sweet chestnut, and belongs to a different family entirely. Its glossy seeds are mildly poisonous to people and horses alike.

hints: A small gnarled evergreen that is the emblem of an entire sea's cuisine.
Narrow grey-green leaves are silver underneath and flash when the wind turns them.
Trunks become hollow and twisted with age, yet the tree keeps fruiting.
Some cultivated groves have been productive for over a thousand years.
Its oil-rich fruit is inedibly bitter until cured in brine or lye.
puzzles.fact: The fruit is far too bitter to eat straight from the tree — it has to be cured in brine, lye or dry salt first, a process attested for at least 6,000 years around the Mediterranean.

hints: A tree of dry savannah with a trunk wildly out of proportion to its crown.
For much of the year it stands bare, the branches looking like roots in the air.
The swollen trunk stores water and can be many metres across.
Local names call it the upside-down tree.
Its large dry fruit is now sold worldwide as a tart, vitamin-C-rich powder.
puzzles.fact: The swollen trunk can hold over 100,000 litres of water, letting it survive months of drought. Hollowed specimens have served as shops, chapels and even a bus shelter.

hints: A slim pale-barked tree of North American mountains that turns whole hillsides gold in autumn.
Its round leaves sit on flattened stalks, so the slightest breeze sets them shivering.
It spreads by root suckers, so a whole grove is often a single organism.
The greenish-white bark photosynthesises, letting it gain energy even in winter sun.
A Utah colony called Pando is among the heaviest and oldest known living organisms.
puzzles.fact: A Utah clone named Pando covers 43 hectares as one organism sharing a single root system, and is estimated to weigh around 6,000 tonnes.

hints: A giant conifer of the Pacific Northwest, second only to one other tree in height.
Its cones hang downward and have three-pointed bracts poking out between the scales.
Those bracts are often described as the back legs and tail of a mouse diving into the cone.
It is not a true member of the genus its common name suggests, hence a Latin prefix meaning 'false'.
It is named after the Scottish botanist who sent seed back to Britain in 1827.
puzzles.fact: Not a true fir at all — its Latin name Pseudotsuga means 'false hemlock'. The common name honours David Douglas, who introduced it to Britain in 1827.

hints: Its smooth grey trunk is notorious for attracting carved initials.
Dense summer shade means almost nothing grows on the woodland floor beneath it.
Young leaves are bright lime green with silky hairs along the margin.
Clipped hedges of it hold their coppery dead leaves right through winter.
Its small triangular nuts, called mast, are produced heavily only every few years.
puzzles.fact: It fruits in irregular 'mast years', flooding the forest floor with nuts every few seasons so that seed predators cannot possibly eat the whole crop at once.

hints: Not really a tree in the usual sense, but the tallest plant of its desert.
It grows in the Mojave and nowhere else.
Stiff dagger-like leaves cluster at the ends of thick, shaggy limbs.
It only branches after a stem has flowered or been damaged.
Settlers said the limbs looked like a biblical prophet raising his arms in prayer, and a US national park carries the name.
puzzles.fact: It depends almost entirely on a single insect, the yucca moth, which deliberately packs pollen into the flower and lays its eggs in the ovary — neither species can reproduce without the other.

hints: A tall single-stemmed desert plant grown in oases for thousands of years.
Its trunk is a rough column of old leaf bases, with no branches at all.
Feather-shaped fronds up to five metres long form a crown at the very top.
Male and female plants are separate, and growers hand-pollinate for a reliable crop.
Its sweet sticky fruit is a staple across North Africa and the Middle East.
puzzles.fact: Cultivated for at least 5,000 years, it is among the oldest domesticated fruit crops. One mature tree can yield over 100 kg of fruit a year for a century.

hints: An evergreen Mediterranean tree grown as much for its bark as its wood.
That bark is thick, spongy and deeply corrugated, and regrows after harvest.
Freshly stripped trunks glow orange-red for months before weathering grey.
The bark is peeled by hand roughly every nine years without killing the tree.
Portugal and Spain supply most of the world's wine-bottle stoppers from it.
puzzles.fact: The bark is stripped by hand every nine years or so and grows back, making it one of very few commercial products harvested repeatedly from a living tree without felling it.

hints: An unmistakable evergreen from the volcanic slopes of Chile and Argentina.
Branches radiate in whorls and curve upward, leaving the lower trunk bare with age.
Every branch is armoured in stiff, sharp, overlapping triangular scales.
It is Chile's national tree, and its large seeds are a traditional food of the Pehuenche people.
Its English name comes from a Victorian joke about which animal would struggle to climb it.
puzzles.fact: The English name comes from a Victorian visitor's remark that the spiny branches would baffle any climbing animal. It is Chile's national tree and now endangered in the wild.

hints: The archetypal big-city street tree of Europe, chosen for its tolerance of pollution.
Its bark flakes off in irregular plates, leaving a camouflage pattern of cream, olive and grey.
Shedding that bark is how it sheds the soot and grime it has absorbed.
Bristly spherical fruits hang on long stalks through winter, usually in pairs.
It is a hybrid, probably raised in seventeenth-century Spain, and its leaves resemble a maple's.
puzzles.fact: A hybrid of two species from opposite sides of the Atlantic. It survives in cities partly because shedding its bark in plates also sheds the pollutants absorbed along with it.

hints: A dark, dense evergreen most often found in old churchyards.
Nearly every part of it is highly poisonous, except the fleshy red cup around the seed.
Its close-grained, springy wood made the medieval longbow.
Trunks become fluted and hollow with age, making them nearly impossible to date by rings.
Some British specimens are thought to be well over 2,000 years old.
puzzles.fact: Its trunk hollows out with age, so ring-counting fails entirely and the oldest British specimens can only be estimated — several are thought to predate the churchyards built around them.

hints: A small layered ornamental tree grown almost entirely for the colour of its foliage.
Hundreds of named cultivars exist, from deep purple to lime green to nearly thread-like leaves.
Palmate leaves are cut deeply into five to nine pointed lobes.
It is a centrepiece of traditional gardens in its home country and a favourite subject for bonsai.
Autumn viewing of its colour, momijigari, is a national pastime there.
puzzles.fact: Autumn leaf-viewing, momijigari, is a centuries-old tradition built largely around this tree, and the colour front is still tracked each year as it moves south across Japan.

hints: A massive evergreen whose flat tiered branches make an unmistakable silhouette on country estates.
Needles grow in dense rosettes on short spurs, and barrel-shaped cones sit upright on the branches.
Its fragrant, rot-resistant timber was traded across the ancient Near East.
The temple of Solomon and the Phoenician fleet were both said to be built from it.
The tree appears on a national flag.
puzzles.fact: It appears on the flag of Lebanon. The ancient forests were logged for millennia, for Phoenician ships and Egyptian tombs alike, and only scattered protected groves survive.

hints: A South American tree now planted across warm cities worldwide for a few spectacular weeks a year.
Fern-like, doubly divided leaves give it a light feathery crown.
It flowers before the leaves are fully out, covering itself completely.
The blossom is a striking violet-blue, and carpets the pavement beneath.
In Pretoria and Sydney its flowering is a byword for exam season.
puzzles.fact: Native to Argentina and Bolivia, it now defines the spring skyline of Pretoria, Sydney, Lisbon and Mexico City — a rare case of one ornamental tree becoming a civic emblem far from home.

hints: A single tree that can look like an entire grove.
It often begins life in the crown of another tree, then strangles it.
Aerial roots drop from the branches, take root, and thicken into new trunks.
One specimen in India covers several acres and has thousands of supporting trunks.
It is the national tree of India, and its tiny flowers are pollinated inside the fruit by specialised wasps.
puzzles.fact: It spreads sideways indefinitely by dropping aerial roots that thicken into new trunks. The Great Banyan in Kolkata covers over 1.8 hectares and reads as a forest rather than a tree.

hints: The traditional European Christmas tree.
Long cylindrical cones hang downward and fall whole rather than breaking up.
Sharp four-sided needles are set singly on tiny woody pegs, which stay behind after the needles drop.
It is the standard timber and paper species of northern Europe, and the wood of violin soundboards.
A Swedish specimen named Old Tjikko has a root system dated to around 9,500 years.
puzzles.fact: A Swedish specimen called Old Tjikko has a root system radiocarbon-dated to roughly 9,500 years, though its visible stem is much younger — the plant keeps regenerating from the same roots.

hints: It grows only on a few dry, wind-scoured mountain ranges of the American West.
Twisted, stripped trunks often keep just a thin ribbon of living bark.
Harsh conditions and dense resinous wood make it extraordinarily slow-growing and rot-resistant.
Its cones carry a small incurved prickle on each scale.
One individual, Methuselah, has been ring-dated to over 4,800 years.
puzzles.fact: A specimen named Methuselah has been dated by ring count to more than 4,800 years, among the oldest known non-clonal organisms. Its exact location in California is undisclosed.

hints: A glossy evergreen of the American South, planted worldwide against warm walls.
Leaves are thick and leathery, dark above and often rust-brown and felted beneath.
Enormous creamy flowers up to 30 cm across smell faintly of lemon.
Its genus evolved before bees existed, and the tough flowers are built for beetles.
It is both the state flower and the state tree of Mississippi.
puzzles.fact: Its genus is old enough to predate bees, so the flowers are beetle-pollinated. That is why the petals are unusually tough and the flower parts sit in a simple spiral rather than distinct whorls.

hints: A small tree grown for a single week of spring, and tracked on national weather forecasts.
Pale pink buds open to almost-white five-petalled blossom before the leaves appear.
It is a sterile hybrid, so every tree is a graft or cutting from the same original.
Japan gave 3,000 of them to Washington DC in 1912, and they still ring the Tidal Basin.
It is the dominant variety of the hanami festival and of Tokyo's blossom forecast.
puzzles.fact: Almost every specimen is a clone of one original hybrid, which is why a whole avenue blooms and drops within the same few days — the basis of Japan's nationwide blossom forecast.

hints: A tall woodland tree, among the last to come into leaf and the first to lose it.
Winter twigs are stout and grey, tipped with unmistakable sooty-black buds.
Pinnate leaves carry seven to thirteen leaflets on a single stalk.
Its tough, springy, shock-absorbing timber made tool handles, oars and early car frames.
A fungal dieback has killed a large share of Europe's population since the 1990s.
puzzles.fact: Its timber is exceptionally shock-absorbent, hence tool handles, hockey sticks and the frames of early cars. Ash dieback, a fungus arriving from Asia, has since killed a large share of Europe's trees.

hints: A fast-growing Australian evergreen now planted for pulp across four continents.
Bark peels away in long ribbons, leaving a smooth mottled trunk beneath.
Juvenile leaves are rounded and powdery; adult leaves are long, curved, and hang vertically.
Its aromatic oil is distilled for decongestants and cleaning products.
It is the floral emblem of Tasmania, and dominates Californian and Iberian plantations.
puzzles.fact: Its adult leaves hang edge-on to the sun to cut water loss, which is why these woodlands cast so little shade. The volatile oil that makes the tree useful also makes it dangerously flammable.

hints: A conifer that drops every needle each autumn, turning foxy orange first.
Its trunk is deeply fluted, with armpit-like hollows beneath each branch.
It was described from fossils before anyone knew it was still alive.
A surviving population was found in a remote Chinese valley in the 1940s.
Seed collected in 1948 was distributed worldwide, and nearly every planted specimen descends from it.
puzzles.fact: Known only from fossils until living trees were found in Hubei, China, in the 1940s. Seed sent abroad in 1948 is the ancestor of virtually every specimen planted anywhere since.
